entitle

/en-TY-tuhl/ - the stress falls on TY · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Entitle means to give someone the right to have or do something.

Twenty years of service entitle every ranger to a lifetime pass through any gate in the park system.

Example

Her grandfather's will entitles each grandchild to one item from the workshop before the auction — Ada chose the dented level that had built three barns.

Entitle creates a claim you can stand on: if a warranty entitles you to repairs, the shop is not doing you a favor — it owes you. Permission can be revoked and kindness can run out, but an entitlement must be honored until the rule that granted it changes.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

license: A license is official permission from an authority, recorded on paper — a credential that certifies you may drive, fish, or practice medicine. Entitle is broader and needs no certificate: a ticket stub, a warranty, or a will can entitle you, creating a claim that must be honored.

permit: To permit is simply to allow — a favor or leave that can be taken back whenever the giver pleases. Entitle creates a standing right instead: once a rule or a purchase serves to entitle you to something, it is owed to you until the rule itself changes.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

disqualify: to strip someone of a claim they held or were building

bar: to shut someone out of the thing altogether

Where it sits · how firmly the outcome is assured

allow → entitle → guarantee

allow vs. entitle: Allow stops short of entitle — what is allowed today can be forbidden tomorrow; a right must be honored.

guarantee vs. entitle: Guarantee goes further than entitle — an entitled customer may claim the refund; a guaranteed one receives it without asking.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — en-: in; cause to have

Root — title: a claim of right - Latin titulus

Put it together: En- (cause to have) + titulus (a title) = to give someone title. In law your title to a house is your documented right to it; entitle hands that kind of claim over, whether the prize is land, a refund, or a lifetime pass. The same titulus gives books their titles — both senses are 'the name that establishes the claim.'

Use the root in a new word: titular: By the end, even the shareholder newsletters described the aging chairman as titular, and nobody at headquarters objected.

Root Check

Word Choice

legal / everyday

Entitle is the general-purpose right-granter: tickets, warranties, bylaws, wills. Reach for its unit-mate enfranchise only when the right in question is the vote. And note the modern edge on entitled — 'he acted entitled' means he claimed rights nobody granted; the verb itself stays neutral.
